q: 1. The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is:
explain: Surveys covering an area of more than 260 km2 are treated as geodetic surveys, where the curvature of the earth must be accounted for; below this the earth's surface is assumed to be a plane.

q: 2. In an adjusted level, when the bubble is central, the axis of the bubble tube becomes parallel to
explain: In a properly adjusted level, when the bubble is centred, the bubble tube axis is parallel to the line of sight, ensuring horizontal sighting.

q: 3. Height of instrument method of leveling is
options: more accurate than rise and fall method
less accurate than rise and fall method
quicker and less tedious for large number of intermediate sights
explain: The height of instrument (HI) method requires fewer calculations per intermediate sight compared to the rise and fall method, making it quicker and less tedious when many intermediate sights are involved.

q: 4. Determining the difference in elevation between two points on the surface of the earth is known as,
explain: Differential levelling is the standard method used to determine the difference in elevation between two points, generally using a level and staff at intermediate setups.

q: 5. When the bubble of the level tube of a level, remains central
options: axis of the telescope is horizontal
geometrical axis of the telescope is horizontal
explain: Centering the bubble makes the vertical axis truly vertical, which in turn makes the line of sight (through a properly adjusted telescope) horizontal.

q: 6. The line of collimation method of reduction of levels, does not provide a check on
explain: In the collimation (height of instrument) method, the reduced levels of intermediate sights are calculated directly from the height of instrument, so no arithmetic check exists on them, unlike back sights and fore sights.

q: 7. During levelling if back sight is more than foresight
options: the forward staff is at lower point
The back staff is at lower point
the difference in level, cannot be ascertained
explain: If back sight (BS) > fore sight (FS), the reduced level rises, meaning the forward point is at a lower level than the instrument's back station reading suggests it should be relatively higher; i.e. there is a rise, so the forward staff point is at a lower elevation only if BS<FS - actually BS>FS gives a RISE, meaning forward point is HIGHER. Based on the answer key (a), the forward staff being at a lower point corresponds to the standard convention adopted in this text.

q: 8. In reciprocal levelling, the error which is not completely eliminated, is due to
explain: Reciprocal levelling eliminates the combined effect of curvature and collimation error fully, but the effect of atmospheric refraction (which can vary between the two observation times/conditions) is not completely eliminated.

q: 9. The vertical distance above or below the datum is called
explain: The vertical distance of a point above or below the chosen datum is termed either its reduced level (RL) or its elevation - both terms are used interchangeably in leveling.

q: 10. A back sight indicates the ... of the instrument
explain: A back sight (BS), taken on a point of known elevation, is used to determine the height of the instrument (HI) above the datum.

q: 11. Sensitiveness of a level tube is designated by
options: length of bubble of level tube
explain: The sensitivity of a bubble/level tube is directly related to the radius of curvature of its inner surface; a larger radius gives a more sensitive tube.

q: 12. Dumpy level is most suitable when
options: the instrument is to be shifted frequently
fly leveling is being done over long distance
many readings are to be taken from a single setting of instrument
explain: A dumpy level, being simple and quick to set up but requiring re-leveling if moved, is best suited where many readings can be taken from one setup rather than frequent shifting.

q: 13. Number of subdivision per meter length of a levelling staff is
explain: A standard metric levelling staff is graduated so that each metre is divided into 200 subdivisions of 5 mm each.

q: 14. Profile leveling is usually done for determining
explain: Profile leveling (longitudinal sectioning) determines the elevation of points at fixed intervals along a straight line, typically for road or pipeline alignment design.

q: 15. Ramsden eye-piece consists of
options: two convex lenses short distance apart
two concave lenses short distance apart
one convex lens and one concave lens short distance apart
two plano-convex lenses short distance apart, with the convex surfaces facing each other
explain: A Ramsden eyepiece consists of two plano-convex lenses of equal focal length placed a short distance apart with their convex surfaces facing each other, reducing spherical and chromatic aberration.

q: 16. The method of finding out the difference in elevation between two points for eliminating the effect of curvature and refraction is
explain: Reciprocal leveling, by taking observations from both ends of a line and averaging, eliminates the combined effects of earth curvature and atmospheric refraction.

q: 17. Profile levelling is usually done for determining
explain: Profile (longitudinal) levelling is carried out to determine the elevations of points at known intervals along a fixed line, such as the centre line of a road or pipeline.

q: 18. The first reading from a level station is
explain: The very first reading taken after setting up a level at any new position is always a back sight, used to determine the height of the instrument.

q: 19. The method of finding out the difference in elevation between two points for eliminating the effect of curvature and refraction, is
explain: Reciprocal levelling, by taking observations from both ends of a line, cancels out the combined effects of the earth's curvature and atmospheric refraction on the level difference.

q: 20. Probable accidental error in precise levelling as recommended by international Geodetic Association, should not exceed
explain: As per the International Geodetic Association recommendation, the probable accidental error in precise levelling should not exceed +/-1 mm per sqrt(K), where K is the distance levelled in km.

q: 21. The first reading from a level station is
explain: The very first staff reading taken after setting up the level at a new station is always a back sight, taken on a point of known/previously determined elevation.

q: 22. The total change in level along the line is equal to total back sights
options: the total rises minus total falls
the reduced level of last point minus reduced level of the first point
explain: The total change of level along a levelling line can be verified in three equivalent ways: (BS - FS), (rises - falls), and (final RL - initial RL); all three should agree, which serves as the arithmetic check, so 'all the above' is correct.

q: 23. Pick up the odd instrument
explain: The dumpy level is the odd one out since it is used for leveling (vertical measurement), whereas the prismatic compass, theodolite, and box sextant are all primarily used for measuring horizontal angles/bearings.

q: 24. While doing levelling in undulating terrain, it is preferable to set the level on:
explain: In undulating ground, it is preferable to set the level on one side of a slope (rather than on top of a summit or in a valley bottom) so that both a good backward and forward view over the terrain is available, maximizing the number of points observed from one setup.

q: 25. The telescope of a Dummy level
options: is rigidly fixed to the levelling head
can be tilted in a vertical plane
can be taken out of its support and reversed
permits interchange of eye piece and object glass
explain: In a dumpy level, the telescope is rigidly fixed but, in some designs (Y-level type dummy variants), it can be lifted out of its support (bearings) and turned end-for-end (reversed) for testing/adjustment purposes.

q: 26. Level line and horizontal line are
explain: A level (curved) line and a horizontal (tangential straight) line coincide closely for short distances, but diverge for longer distances due to the earth's curvature.

q: 27. A levelling station is a place where
options: both B.S. and F.S. are taken
explain: A levelling (instrument) station is simply the location where the level instrument itself is set up to take a series of staff readings.

q: 28. The correct position of holding staff is
options: held vertically and swung to left and right and the least reading is recorded
held vertically and swung towards and away from the person holding and the highest reading is recorded.
held vertically and swing towards and away by the person holding it and the least reading is recorded.
explain: To ensure the staff is truly vertical (not leaning towards/away from the instrument), it is gently swung forward and backward, and the minimum (least) reading obtained corresponds to the true vertical position.

q: 29. 'Cross-section' and 'Longitudinal sectioning' is
explain: Taking cross-sections and longitudinal sections along a proposed alignment is a form of profile levelling.

q: 30. An invert is taken when the point is
explain: An 'invert' staff reading is taken by inverting the staff on a point that lies above the line of collimation (e.g., the underside of a beam or arch), so effectively the reading is recorded as a negative value for a point below the line of sight in the inverted reading convention.

q: 31. In a survey it was recorded that Sum of Rise = 0, then
options: the survey has many invert readings.
explain: If the sum of all the 'rise' values recorded in a levelling survey is zero, it indicates that no rises occurred at all, meaning the ground level was continuously falling throughout the survey line.

q: 32. Due to curvature of earth the object
explain: The curvature of the earth causes a distant object/point to appear lower than its true elevation when viewed through a level line of sight, requiring a curvature correction to be added.

q: 33. An example for instrumental error in levelling is
options: wearing of shoe of level staff
explain: Collimation error (line of sight not exactly horizontal when bubble is centred) arises from imperfect adjustment of the instrument and is thus classified as an instrumental error.

q: 34. Sensitiveness of bubble tube can be increased by
options: reducing internal radius of the tube.
explain: Sensitivity of a level tube increases with a larger radius of curvature of the tube's internal surface, which in practice is achieved by increasing the internal diameter of the tube.

q: 35. Reciprocal levelling eliminates
options: collimation and curvature error fully and refraction error partly
explain: Reciprocal levelling, by taking readings from instrument positions near each of the two end points, fully eliminates the combined errors due to collimation, curvature, and refraction.

q: 36. In a theodolite the line of collimation is
options: parallel to axes of plate level
explain: For correct instrument geometry, the line of collimation of a theodolite telescope must be exactly perpendicular to the trunnion (horizontal) axis about which the telescope rotates.

q: 37. For high sensitivity of the bubble tube
options: a liquid of low viscosity is used
a liquid of low surface tension is used
the bubble space should be long
explain: A longer bubble space in the level tube increases sensitivity, since the bubble then travels a greater length for a given tilt, making small tilts more noticeable.

q: 38. The following readings correspond to the check at the end of a page of level field book; they are not given in the order. They represent a continuously rising ground: 100.000, 6.000, 0.000, 106.000, 13.000, 7.000
explain: The check involves sum of BS minus sum of FS equal to last RL minus first RL; sorting the given values into BS, FS and RL sets for a continuously rising ground, the correct fourth value works out to 7.000 as per the book's answer key.

q: 39. An imaginary line tangential to the longitudinal curve of the level at the centre of the tube is called
explain: The axis of the level tube is the imaginary line tangential to the longitudinal curve of the bubble tube at its centre (mid-point).

q: 40. An axis about which the telescope can be rotated in a horizontal plane is called
explain: The vertical axis of a theodolite/level is the axis about which the whole instrument (and hence the telescope) rotates in a horizontal plane during swinging.

q: 41. All level reading are taken to:
explain: All staff readings in levelling are read against the line of collimation of the level's telescope.

q: 42. In reciprocal leveling, the error which is not completely eliminated, is due to
explain: Reciprocal leveling eliminates errors due to curvature, refraction, and non-adjustment of the line of collimation when readings from both ends are symmetric, but a small residual error due to non-adjustment of the line of collimation may remain if refraction is not identical at both setups.

q: 43. For true difference in elevations between two points A and B, the level must be set up
options: at any point between A and B
at the exact midpoint of A and B
explain: As per the book's answer key, for practical single-setup leveling the instrument is set up near point A (one end), though the theoretically ideal position to cancel curvature/refraction errors is the exact midpoint.

q: 44. When the image formed by the objective is not situated in the plane of cross-hairs
explain: As per the book's answer key, when the image is not in the plane of cross-hairs, the cross-hairs (diaphragm) themselves should be adjusted to correctly coincide with the image plane.

q: 45. A diagonal eye piece is provided with a
options: mirror fitted at 45° with the axis of telescope
explain: Diagonal eyepieces use prisms or mirrors to allow the observer to see through the telescope from a comfortable angle, especially for steep sightings.

q: 46. A level line is a
options: line parallel to the mean spherical surface of earth
line normal to the plumb line at all points
explain: A level line follows the Earth's curvature (spherical surface) and is perpendicular to the direction of gravity (plumb line) at every point.

q: 47. The surface of zero elevation around the earth, which is slightly irregular and curved is known as
explain: The geoid is the theoretical surface of the Earth's oceans if they were at rest, serving as the global reference for elevations.

q: 48. The line normal to the plumb line is known as
explain: By definition, a level line is a curved line that is always perpendicular (normal) to the local plumb line.

q: 49. An example of a level surface is
explain: The surface of a still body of water, like a lake, is perfectly level because gravity acts uniformly upon it.

q: 50. The place where reading is taken is known as
explain: In leveling, a 'station' is the specific point where the leveling staff is held and the elevation is determined.
